claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a self-healing chromium- and nickel-rich passive oxide film.
The passive film dynamically restores itself under simultaneous chemical and irradiation stresses.
The starting steels have conventional microstructures and contain alloying elements such as Cr and Ni without an intentionally optimized passive film.
Controlled heat treatment and surface pretreatment can enhance Cr and Ni segregation at the steel surface.
The treatment will produce a dense, adherent, Cr- and Ni-rich passive oxide film.
A smoother surface favors formation of a compact and protective passive film in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
Cr and Ni preferentially segregate to the steel surface.
Surface-segregated Cr and Ni form the passive oxide layer.
After chemical attack or irradiation damage, the passive layer rapidly re-oxidizes and repairs itself.
A compact passive film acts as a protective barrier that reduces further corrosion of the underlying metal.
Treated steels will have lower corrosion rates than untreated controls.
Treated steels will have higher polarization resistance than untreated controls.
In situ surface analysis will show rapid passive-film reformation after localized damage under both corrosive and irradiation stresses.
Untreated baseline steels have a less stable, non-self-healing passive film.
The proposed mechanism applies across chloride-containing, acidic, and alkaline environments under moderate-to-high irradiation fluxes and operational temperatures and pressures.
Long-term film durability and repair kinetics under sustained combined chemical and irradiation stresses remain uncertain.
Failure to observe a statistically significant corrosion-resistance improvement or rapid passive-film reformation in treated specimens would falsify the hypothesis.
